messages.subject: Finite mixture vs Dirichlet-process mixture
parts:
Dear Nimble devs and users,

I use Nimble for non-parametric population-density inference. So far I have used a finite mixture (of, say, gaussians) with a large (50–200) number N of components. The prior on the component weights is Dirichlet with parameter α/N. If, during the sampling, the number of occupied components is close to N, then I increase N and re-run the sampler; so this mathematical representation if effectively non-parametric. Conjugacy and conjugate Gibbs samplers are used for the components. It has worked quite well so far. Below you find an example skeleton code.

Several works [1] show that this representation is asymptotically equivalent to a Dirichlet-process mixture with concentration parameter α. I am therefore considering using the Dirichlet-process capabilities of Nimble, for example with the dCRP distribution and samplers (chapter 10 in the manual).

Conceptually I don't see much difference between the finite-mixture and Dirichlet-process-mixture representation. With Nimble's dCRP I also need to decide on an upper bound of components and increase it if necessary. But I wonder: would the use of dCRP or stick-breaking lead to faster sampling and mixing? That would be a good reason to change.

From § 10.4 of the manual I can't really understand whether the samplers involved would lead to faster sampling. So best to ask the developers for their insight on this, before embarking on days of testing :) Worth mentioning that matters such as label switching or ordering do not concern me (goal is density inference), so any extra calculations for those would be wasted for me.

Thank you for your insight and tips – and for Nimble!
Cheers,
Luca

My skeleton code:

finitemixture <- nimbleCode({
weights[1:nClusters] ~ ddirch(alpha=alpha0[1:nClusters])
## alpha0 is a vector of alpha/nClusters
##
for(acluster in 1:nClusters){
for(avariate in 1:nVariates){
means[avariate, acluster] ~ ...
variances[avariate, acluster] ~ ...
}
}
for(adatum in 1:nData){
C[adatum] ~ dcat(prob=weights[1:nClusters])
##
for(avariate in 1:nVariates){
Data[adatum, avariate] ~ dnorm(mean=means[avariate,C[adatum]], var=variances[avar,C[adatum]])
}
}
})

[1]
Rousseau & Mengersen
https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2011.00781.x

also Rasmussen
https://www.seas.harvard.edu/courses/cs281/papers/rasmussen-1999a.pdf

and Rossi
https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400850303

messages.subject: Re: Finite mixture vs Dirichlet-process mixture
parts:
Hi Luca,

If the finite mixture is asymptotically equivalent (in particular in terms of favoring fewer clusters a priori) to the Dirichlet process mixture (DPM),  then I think the main question will be computational.

With dCRP in NIMBLE, we only sample the parameters  of the occupied clusters (i.e., only some of the elements of 'means' and 'variances'), which saves time. 
In your finite mixture formulation, NIMBLE will sample all the parameters. If there are many unoccupied clusters, this will be inefficient. 

Also, with dCRP in NIMBLE, we only propose that the cluster membership for a given element be either one of the existing clusters or a single new cluster. With your finite mixture 
formulation, NIMBLE will propose that the cluster membership for a given element be any of the clusters (including all the unoccupied ones) because it will use our categorical sampler.

I suspect this means that using NIMBLE's dCRP will lead to less computation and therefore faster MCMC. (Side note, I suspect convergence/mixing would be similar on a per iteration basis.)

-Chris

Hi Chris,

Fantastic, thank you for the explanation! Then I'll use the dCRP. Quite curious to see how much the sampling will speed up.

And yes, I can confirm the results of Rousseau & Mengersen from my own analyses. I've observed that below a certain value of N in the finite mixture all components tend to be occupied. But from some value onwards (around 50 in my cases), only a finite number of components is used, and they stay the same if N is increased. For all datasets I've been analysing so far it did not make a difference whether N was 64, 128, or 256 – except for computation time of course.

Cheers and thank you for your always insightful and kind help!
Luca

messages.subject: dCPR and categorical components (Was: Finite mixture vs Dirichlet-process mixture)
parts:
Hi Chris & devs,

Following your insight on the dCPR sampler, I've tried to implement it in my case. Compilation and sampling work fine, but I get an error when I run getSamplesDPmeasure() on the compiled model:


Error in mvIndexes[l, (tildeVarsColsSum[j] + 1):tildeVarsColsSum[j + 1]] <- which(aux != :
number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length


I've been trying to find where the problem is, and now my suspicion is the presence of categorical distributions among the component kernels. The infinite mixture is defined as follows:

infmixture <- nimbleCode({
C[1:nData] ~ dCRP(alpha, size=nData)
##
## Hyperparaeters for real variates
for(avar in 1:nRvars){
varRrate[avar] ~ dinvgamma(shape=varRshape1[avar], scale=1)
}
##
## Mixture parameters
for(acluster in 1:nClusters){
## real variates
for(avar in 1:nRvars){
meanR[avar,acluster] ~ dnorm(mean=meanRmean0[avar], var=meanRvar0[avar])
varR[avar,acluster] ~ dinvgamma(shape=varRshape2shape[avar], rate=varRrate[avar])
}
## categorical variates
for(avar in 1:nCvars){
probC[avar,acluster,1:nCategories] ~ ddirch(alpha=calpha0[avar,1:nCategories])
}
## binary variates
for(avar in 1:nBvars){
probB[avar,acluster] ~ dbeta(shape1=probBa0[avar], shape2=probBb0[avar])
}
}
##
## Data
## real variates
for(avar in 1:nRvars){
Real[adatum,avar] ~ dnorm(mean=meanR[avar,C[adatum]], var=varR[avar,C[adatum]])
}
## categorical variates
for(avar in 1:nCvars){
Category[adatum,avar] ~ dcat(prob=probC[avar,C[adatum],1:nCategories])
}
## binary variates
for(avar in 1:nBvars){
Binary[adatum,avar] ~ dbern(prob=probB[avar,C[adatum]])
}
})


There are
• nRvars real variates, with gaussian kernels
• nCvars categorical variates, with categorical-distribution kernels (they all have the same max number of categories)
• nBvars binary variates, with Bernoulli kernels.

each component is the product of all these kernels (this is the very flexible approach explained in Dunson & Bhattacharya https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199694587.003.0005).

I've noticed that if I exclude the categorical kernels, then getSamplesDPmeasure() doesn't throw any errors. Is it possible that the three-index probC parameter:

dcat(prob=probC[avar, C[adatum], 1:nCategories])

is the cause of the problem? In that case, any ideas how I can bypass it? If not I may send you a more complete version of the code.

Cheers!

Luca

It is great that you are using the BNP function in nimble! I’m sorry you are having issued though.

I have seen that for more complicated models, the stick-breaking function mixes better than the dCRP. The MCMC is definitely slower for the stick-breaking, but I think it is worth trying it.

I hope this helps.

Best,
Claudia

Hi Claudia,

Thank you very much for looking into this. A minimal code showing the problem is enclosed. It has a logical variable that lets you test with and without the categorical-kernel components.

While preparing this I've met a new problem when specific settings are used, even without categorical components. See the "NOTE" comment in the code for this – but maybe it's unrelated.


Regarding the stick-breaking alternative, the code in example 10.3.2 of the manual is actually the same as for the finite-mixture representation, except that instead of the lines

for(i in 1:(L-1)){
v[i] ~ dbeta(1, alpha)
}
w[1:L] <- stick_breaking(v[1:(L-1)])

(considering constant alpha for simplicity), the finite mixture has the line

w[1:L] ~ ddirch(alpha=alphavector[1:L])

where alphavector=rep(alpha,L). Indeed the result of Rousseau & Mengersen is that the two representations are equivalent for enough large L. The distribution of the number of occupied clusters becomes the same.

Given this, I don't know whether using stick-breaking would really give any improvements in speed with respect to the finite-mixture that I'm using. What do you think?

Cheers!
Luca

Hi Luca,

I hope this email finds you well!
I looked into your model and I am not sure I understand it completely.

The data in this example is a 5x2 matrix. You have ncluster=10. Does this mean that there could be 10 clusters in your data? What kind of clustering are you trying to do? If you are trying to cluster observations (rows) there should be at most ncluster=5 if you are trying to cluster variables (columns) there should be at most ncluster=2. What am I missing? 

Also, the cluster variables, ‘Rmeans’ and ‘Rvariances’ are of dimension 2x10. How does this relate to the 5x2 dimensional data?

Finally, what is the effect of ‘Cdata’ in the model when includecat=TRUE? Why do you need the third dimension in Cdata?  

Regarding the finite mixture and the truncation of the DP:

When coding the truncated version of the DP, it does seem to be very similar to the finite mixture. But you have to remember that the theoretical definition of the DP is really an infinite mixture, whereas the theoretical definition of the finite mixture model is  a finite mixture model. And so, in finite mixture models you need to specify the fixed number of components somehow. In a DP representation you don’t need to do that. When L goes to infinity the finite mixture representation is equivalent to the infinite stick breaking as you mentioned.  Recall that there are other (than the truncated stick-breaking) ways to represent the DP that don’t rely on a truncation. 

I hope this makes sense.

Best,
Claudia

Hi Claudia, thank you, hope all is well there too!

Very sorry that the code was unclear, I should have explained better.

In this example problem, every datapoint is a tuple of two real variates and two categorical variates; we can write one datapoint as

(x, y, u, v)
x ∈ ℝ, y ∈ ℝ,
u ∈ {'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'},
v ∈ {'A', 'B', 'C', 'D'}

I actually label the categories with integers {1,2,3,4} in each set, but these integer values are meaningless per se: no ordering implied and so on. (These "points" actually represent patients, and the four variates are several kinds of continuous/categorical-ranged biomarkers.)

The code has 5 datapoints as an example, each of which is a quadruple like the above. They are collected in the 5×4 matrix "datapoints".

The purpose is to infer the full-population-frequency distribution in this hybrid continuous-discrete space given the sample of five points (patients).

We mathematically represent this unknown distribution F as the sum of product kernels, with Gaussian kernels N() for the two real variates and categorical kernels C() for the two categorical variates:

F(x, y, u, v) = ∑ wᵢ N(x|αᵢ) N(y|βᵢ) C(u|pᵢ) C(v|qᵢ)

where the w are normalized weights, α and β are each a gaussian parameter pair, and the p and q are each a discrete probability distribution over four points.

If the sum runs to infinity (as in the true DP representation), then this is a non-parametric model. If the sum is finite but large this is a semi-parametric model. If we leave open the possibility of increasing the sum terms if necessary, then this is effectively a non-parametric model.

The unknown population-frequency distribution is then represented by the in-principle infinite tuple ({wᵢ, αᵢ, βᵢ, pᵢ, qᵢ}), and inference is made on this tuple in Nimble.

So yes, we need to have many clusters, more than the data if the data are few – otherwise this would not be a semi- or non-parametric representation.

This mathematical representation is redundant, because different parameter tuples may correspond to the same frequency distribution F. But this is completely fine. Technically speaking we are using a frame, instead of a basis, to represent elements of the function space {F}. We can also say that we are working with probability distributions on a covering of the function space {F}.

This representation is extremely convenient as it allows for the computation of marginals and conditional distributions of any set of variates we want, conditional on any other set (which is what I need in my research). See the enclosed paper by Dunson & Bhattacharya in this regard.

The "clusters" appear as a by-product of this mathematical representation, I don't give them any significance; a bit like the Legendre polynomials in a function representation. Also I don't see how I could give them significance anyway, unless I have good grounds to assume that subpopulations should have Gaussian distributions (why not Cauchy or Gumbel or something else?).

Let me know if this clarifies the code!

> When coding the truncated version of the DP, it does seem to be very similar to the finite mixture. But you have to remember that the theoretical definition of the DP is really an infinite mixture, whereas the theoretical definition of the finite mixture model is  a finite mixture model. And so, in finite mixture models you need to specify the fixed number of components somehow.

Sure, but then also in Nimble the stick_breaking model is actually just a finite-mixture model; it doesn't have an infinite number of components.

The fact that it still works (approximately) as an infinite-mixture model is because of the mathematical theorem saying that if the number L of components is large, and the weights follow a Dirichlet distribution with concentration ~1/L, then the difference between the finite and infinite mixture is small enough in some appropriate norm.

The getSamplesDPmeasure() of the dCRP model is a bit better in this regard, this is why I was interested in using it.

Cheers,
Luca

Thanks for the extra details. So, each data vector is modeled as a product of normal and categorical kernels. 

I see the convenience in doing this to find whatever marginal or conditional you might be interested in.

I agree that using dCRP rather than the stick-breaking seems “more nonparametric”. I do think you will get very similar results with both, even when truncating the random measure. First two columns are for the real variables and the last 2 are for the categorical variables. I wrote a code, please see it attached, based on what you had (I did some changes though). I included the categorical variables. I was able to run the MCMC and use the getSamplesDPmeasure function. I did not try it for other data sets, but I think it should work fine.

> The code has 5 datapoints as an example, each of which is a quadruple like the above. They are collected in the 5×4 matrix "datapoints".
>
> The purpose is to infer the full-population-frequency distribution in this hybrid continuous-discrete space given the sample of five points (patients).
>
> We mathematically represent this unknown distribution F as the sum of product kernels, with Gaussian kernels N() for the two real variates and categorical kernels C() for the two categorical variates:
>
> F(x, y, u, v) = ∑ wᵢ N(x|αᵢ) N(y|βᵢ) C(u|pᵢ) C(v|qᵢ)
>
> where the w are normalized weights, α and β are each a gaussian parameter pair, and the p and q are each a discrete probability distribution over four points.
>
> If the sum runs to infinity (as in the true DP representation), then this is a non-parametric model. If the sum is finite but large this is a semi-parametric model. If we leave open the possibility of increasing the sum terms if necessary, then this is effectively a non-parametric model.
>
> The unknown population-frequency distribution is then represented by the in-principle infinite tuple ({wᵢ, αᵢ, βᵢ, pᵢ, qᵢ}), and inference is made on this tuple in Nimble.
>
> So yes, we need to have many clusters, more than the data if the data are few – otherwise this would not be a semi- or non-parametric representation.
>
> This mathematical representation is redundant, because different parameter tuples may correspond to the same frequency distribution F. But this is completely fine. Technically speaking we are using a frame, instead of a basis, to represent elements of the function space {F}. We can also say that we are working with probability distributions on a covering of the function space {F}.
>
> This representation is extremely convenient as it allows for the computation of marginals and conditional distributions of any set of variates we want, conditional on any other set (which is what I need in my research). See the enclosed paper by Dunson & Bhattacharya in this regard.
>
> The "clusters" appear as a by-product of this mathematical representation, I don't give them any significance; a bit like the Legendre polynomials in a function representation. Also I don't see how I could give them significance anyway, unless I have good grounds to assume that subpopulations should have Gaussian distributions (why not Cauchy or Gumbel or something else?).
>
> Let me know if this clarifies the code!
>
>
>> When coding the truncated version of the DP, it does seem to be very similar to the finite mixture. But you have to remember that the theoretical definition of the DP is really an infinite mixture, whereas the theoretical definition of the finite mixture model is  a finite mixture model. And so, in finite mixture models you need to specify the fixed number of components somehow.
>
> Sure, but then also in Nimble the stick_breaking model is actually just a finite-mixture model; it doesn't have an infinite number of components.
>
> The fact that it still works (approximately) as an infinite-mixture model is because of the mathematical theorem saying that if the number L of components is large, and the weights follow a Dirichlet distribution with concentration ~1/L, then the difference between the finite and infinite mixture is small enough in some appropriate norm.
>
> The getSamplesDPmeasure() of the dCRP model is a bit better in this regard, this is why I was interested in using it.
>
> Cheers,
> Luca

Hi Claudia,

Fantastic, thank you for your time and patience!

This particular product kernel is widely used in situations where you have variates of a mixed kind. The fact that I'm working with it testifies to the great flexibility of Nimble. At the moment, no package in any scripting language allows us to work with this kind of probability structures. If it hadn't been for Nimble I would have had to code this myself in C or similar. Nimble has been a real life changer.

I'm trying your code and it seems to work, thank you! There's one drawback: in the original version all parameters have conjugate relationships, and Nimble recognizes this conjugate structure. Now it is assigning random-walk samplers, and I don't seem to manage to change those. Probably I have to write a conjugate sampler as explained in the manual?
> theoretical world :) Just a note: even when using the dCRP you will never get more clusters than data points you have.

In the dCRP, the getSamplesDPmeasure() function draws from the base hyperdistribution, and this is effectively the rest of the clusters combined, so this is not a problem.

I have seen that stick_breaking also allows me to use more components than data (if necessary). So no problems there either.

Unless you mean that the data cannot belong to all available clusters; yes of course many components are empty then. These empty components are important: they show (and quantify) the large model uncertainty that we have in situations with very few data. It's the uncertainty that parametric models (and old frequentist methods) swipe under the carpet. I work with researchers, especially from the medical field, that are switching from old methods, and they are surprised seeing how large uncertainties are actually there – but they are also happy to be making more honest assessments about their results. All this is again thanks to Nimble.

Cheers!
Luca
